claims.statement: The EU Data Act applies since 12 September 2025 and covers raw and pre-processed data from connected products that is readily available to the data holder.

Users can ask a data holder to share connected-product data with a chosen third party, but personal-data disclosure still requires a valid legal basis and trade-secret or safety safeguards may restrict sharing.
Chapter II generally exempts data generated by connected products made or designed by qualifying micro and small enterprises, narrowing the original small-OEM target.
The Commission has published voluntary model terms for data-holder, user and data-recipient relationships, so the necessary contractual roles are operationally definable but must still be agreed.

Steelbridge publicly offers an almost identical Data Act compliance layer with consent, third-party access, APIs, audit logs and white labelling at published self-serve tiers of EUR 250, EUR 500 and EUR 750 per month.
IoT and servitization platforms already advertise native Data Act access, authorization, audit and export capabilities, creating a strong bundling threat.
Adjacent privacy-rights suites already automate intake, identity verification, retrieval and secure response, reducing novelty in the generic request-workflow layer.

contrary_evidence: Steelbridge markets the same core compliance infrastructure and white-label model, with public pricing close to the proposed base fee.
Qualifying micro and small connected-product manufacturers are generally outside the Chapter II obligation, weakening the original small-OEM segment.
dDruid and Servitly bundle Data Act access and authorization into broader IoT or after-sales platforms that already sit on telemetry.
OneTrust already productizes identity verification, request intake and secure fulfillment for adjacent data-rights workflows.
The founder's family installer can validate heat-pump service pain but is not itself an OEM data holder and cannot grant telemetry rights.

fingerprint.compounding_advantage: contract-permitted library of device schemas, identity proofs and adjudicated entitlement patterns, with cross-OEM reuse limited to non-confidential abstractions
fingerprint.customer: non-exempt mid-market connected-equipment OEMs lacking a production Data Act access operation; qualifying micro and small manufacturers are not assumed to be mandatory buyers
fingerprint.distribution_mechanism: one vertical OEM design partner followed by authorized IoT-platform, warranty-administrator and equipment-service referrals
fingerprint.offer_and_business_model: OEM-branded intake, device-user mapping, policy controls, audit and scoped export operating inside the OEM's contracted telemetry boundary
fingerprint.payer_and_paid_event: OEM pays a production-interface subscription and onboarding fee; device and request meters remain optional until real volumes are measured
fingerprint.problem_trigger: a connected-product user or authorized third party requests raw or pre-processed data that the OEM holds

founder_fit: Good technical fit with the founder's data-platform, privacy-aware automation and anomaly-detection skills.
The renewable-energy family network can expose heat-pump installation and service use cases, but it does not supply the essential OEM telemetry contract or enterprise buyer.

A one-OEM read-only pilot could fit the founder's part-time and PLN 100000 constraints under the UNVALIDATED HYPOTHESIS that capital_required_pln=70000 is sufficient; enterprise selling, legal review and security response must be delegated rather than becoming continuous founder work.
risks: An identity or entitlement error could disclose personal, industrial or trade-secret data.
An OEM may be exempt, already compliant, or able to enable the same feature in its incumbent IoT platform.
A platform contract may prohibit the telemetry access or cross-customer learning needed for delivery and compounding.
Security, safety or trade-secret objections can require suspension or human adjudication, increasing support cost.
A direct competitor can anchor pricing and copy a narrow vertical implementation before a proprietary dataset forms.

structure.control_point: contracted identity and entitlement gate immediately before an OEM releases connected-product data
structure.critical_dependency: a signed OEM or authorized IoT-platform agreement granting telemetry access plus reliable device-to-user identity mapping

thesis: Provide a narrowly scoped, OEM-branded Data Act access operation for a non-exempt mid-market connected-equipment maker, starting with one heat-pump or energy-equipment device family. The service operates only inside an OEM-authorized telemetry boundary: it authenticates the requester, maps the device to the user, applies personal-data, trade-secret and safety controls, logs the decision and exports only raw or pre-processed data the OEM holds. The OEM remains the data holder and any controller; the gateway claims no independent entitlement. A durable advantage is possible only if contracts permit reuse of non-confidential schema and adjudication patterns, because direct specialist and IoT-platform competitors already sell the core layer.
title: Connected-Equipment Data Entitlement Gateway
uncertainties: Observed request volume by device family and whether compliance urgency converts into software budget
Whether a target OEM is legally in scope rather than covered by the micro or small-enterprise exemption
Whether OEM and IoT-cloud contracts grant the access, processor role and audit rights needed for a pilot
Acceptable identity proof where ownership, rental, installer and service-provider roles overlap
Which schema and adjudication learnings may be reused across OEMs without breaching confidentiality or data-protection duties
Actual data-egress, security-review, support, insurance and enterprise acquisition costs
